If you own Palo Alto firewalls, Cortex is the stronger answer. If endpoint is your centre of gravity and you want human hunters, CrowdStrike is. Microsoft Defender XDR vs everyone. In an E5 estate, Defender XDR is close to free and genuinely good across Microsoft’s surface. The question is never whether it’s adequate it usually is but whether concentrating detection with your productivity vendor is acceptable, and what your third-party data costs once you add Sentinel. XDR vs SIEM. They overlap and increasingly converge. XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with less engineering effort; SIEM ingests everything including non-security logs and requires you to build detections. Most mature organizations run both. Small teams should start with XDR, because a SIEM nobody has time to tune produces nothing. Buyer’s Guide Audit your telemetry sources before taking quotes. List every source you need correlated endpoints, firewalls, email, identity provider, cloud accounts, SaaS applications and mark which are native to each vendor. That table decides your shortlist faster than any feature comparison. Model ingestion cost explicitly. XDR pricing is increasingly data-volume-driven, and this is where budgets break. Get a written estimate based on your actual log volume, with a stated overage policy. Measure alert reduction in the proof of concept. The metric that matters is incidents per week that require analyst attention, compared with what your current tooling produces. If XDR doesn’t reduce that number, it hasn’t done its job. Decide the native-versus-open question first. It’s architectural and it determines everything downstream, including whether the platform you buy will still fit in three years. Common mistakes: buying XDR while leaving identity telemetry out of scope, when identity is where most modern attacks progress; assuming XDR replaces the need for managed detection and response when nobody is watching overnight; and paying platform prices to correlate third-party data poorly. Frequently Asked Questions What is XDR? Extended detection and response correlates security telemetry from multiple sources endpoints, network, email, identity, and cloud into unified incidents, applying analytics across the combined data rather than treating each source separately. The goal is fewer, higher-quality incidents instead of more alerts from more consoles. What is the best XDR platform in 2026? Palo Alto Cortex XDR scores highest on data coverage and correlation depth, with CrowdStrike close behind on detection engineering and threat intelligence. Microsoft Defender XDR is the rational choice for Microsoft 365 E5 organizations, and SentinelOne Singularity offers the strongest response automation for small teams. What is the difference between XDR and SIEM? XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with detection content the vendor provides and maintains. SIEM ingests logs from anywhere, including non-security sources, and generally requires you to build and tune your own detections. XDR is faster to value; SIEM is more flexible and better for compliance log retention. Many organizations run both. What is open XDR versus native XDR? Native XDR correlates telemetry the vendor collects with its own products, giving deeper and faster correlation at the cost of vendor consolidation. Open XDR treats third-party telemetry as a first-class source, letting you keep existing tools with generally shallower correlation. Choose based on how standardized your estate already is. Do I need XDR if I have EDR? Not necessarily. If endpoints are your main risk surface and your team is small, good EDR with strong automation may be sufficient. Modern Extended Detection and Response (XDR) solutions correlates signals from endpoints, network, email, identity, and cloud into single investigable incidents reducing alert volume rather than adding another console.

How We Scored

A structured research-based evaluation, not a comparative lab test, and we claim no testing. Five criteria weighted for what determines whether XDR reduces work or adds to it:

• Data coverage (25%) — how many telemetry sources are natively supported: endpoint, network, email, identity, cloud, SaaS, and OT.

• Correlation quality (25%) — how effectively raw signals become a small number of high-fidelity incidents. This is the entire point of XDR and where platforms differ most.

• Response automation (20%) — playbooks, automated containment, and how much can happen without an analyst.

• Openness (15%) — whether third-party data sources are genuinely first-class or grudgingly supported. This determines whether XDR fits your estate or requires you to rebuild it.

• Operability (15%) — how much expertise the platform demands day to day.

Published MITRE ATT&CK Evaluation results informed the correlation and coverage assessments; we did not conduct our own testing.

The Question That Should Decide Your Shortlist

Native XDR or open XDR?

Native XDR — Palo Alto, CrowdStrike, Microsoft, SentinelOne, Trend Micro correlates telemetry the vendor collects itself. Correlation is deeper and faster because the vendor controls the data format end to end. The cost is consolidation: you get the most value by buying that vendor’s endpoint, network, and cloud products too.

Open XDR ingests third-party telemetry as a first-class citizen, letting you keep the tools you have. Correlation is generally shallower because the data is less consistent, but you avoid a rip-and-replace.

The honest guidance: If you are already substantially standardized on one of the big platform vendors, native XDR gives you dramatically better outcomes for less effort.

If your estate is genuinely heterogeneous and will stay that way, an open approach or a modern SIEM with automation and detection engineering is usually the more realistic answer than pretending a native platform will correlate your other vendors’ data well.

The trap to avoid: buying a native XDR platform and then feeding it third-party data via generic connectors. You pay platform prices for SIEM-quality correlation. Decide which model you’re in before you take quotes.

Head-to-Head Comparisons Buyers Actually Make

Microsoft Defender XDR vs everyone. In an E5 estate, Defender XDR is close to free and genuinely good across Microsoft’s surface.

XDR vs SIEM. They overlap and increasingly converge. XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with less engineering effort; SIEM ingests everything including non-security logs and requires you to build detections.

Most mature organizations run both. Small teams should start with XDR, because a SIEM nobody has time to tune produces nothing.

Buyer’s Guide

Audit your telemetry sources before taking quotes. List every source you need correlated endpoints, firewalls, email, identity provider, cloud accounts, SaaS applications and mark which are native to each vendor. That table decides your shortlist faster than any feature comparison.

Model ingestion cost explicitly. XDR pricing is increasingly data-volume-driven, and this is where budgets break. Get a written estimate based on your actual log volume, with a stated overage policy.

Decide the native-versus-open question first. It’s architectural and it determines everything downstream, including whether the platform you buy will still fit in three years.

Common mistakes: buying XDR while leaving identity telemetry out of scope, when identity is where most modern attacks progress; assuming XDR replaces the need for managed detection and response when nobody is watching overnight; and paying platform prices to correlate third-party data poorly.

Frequently Asked Questions What is XDR?

Extended detection and response correlates security telemetry from multiple sources endpoints, network, email, identity, and cloud into unified incidents, applying analytics across the combined data rather than treating each source separately.

The goal is fewer, higher-quality incidents instead of more alerts from more consoles.

XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with detection content the vendor provides and maintains. SIEM ingests logs from anywhere, including non-security sources, and generally requires you to build and tune your own detections.

XDR is faster to value; SIEM is more flexible and better for compliance log retention. Many organizations run both.

What is open XDR versus native XDR?

Native XDR correlates telemetry the vendor collects with its own products, giving deeper and faster correlation at the cost of vendor consolidation.

Open XDR treats third-party telemetry as a first-class source, letting you keep existing tools with generally shallower correlation. Choose based on how standardized your estate already is.

CrowdStrike is the pick when endpoint detection quality and managed hunting matter most, SentinelOne when automation must substitute for headcount, and Microsoft Defender XDR when you already hold E5 the economics there are hard to argue with.

How a WAF Works

A WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic using predefined rules or policies to detect malicious patterns. Here’s how it operates:

  • Traffic Inspection: It examines HTTP methods (e.g., GET, POST), headers, query strings, and request bodies for suspicious activity.
  • Filtering Models:
  • Negative Security Model: Blocks known malicious patterns or signatures.
  • Positive Security Model: Allows only known legitimate traffic while scrutinizing anomalies.
  • Real-Time Blocking: Malicious requests are blocked before reaching the web server, while legitimate traffic is allowed through.
  • Data Protection: Prevents sensitive data leakage by masking or blocking certain responses.
  • Deployment Modes: Commonly deployed as a reverse proxy, ensuring all traffic passes through the WAF for inspection.

items.summary: Here it is! :) One of my main goals for 2026 has arrived a little later than expected, but it is finally here: the CYBER HUNTER PROJECT book. I have to say that writing a book from scratch has been quite an adventure. I have learned a lot about all the challenges and difficulties involved in taking an idea and turning it into a published book. I hope you enjoy it — and if you decide to grab a copy, you will be helping me turn all that effort into a well-earned beer or coffee! 🍺☕ Why I Wrote This Book Over the years, I have created many hunts to investigate real situations. Some started with an alert, others with a suspicion, and quite a few with a simple thought: what if this is happening in my environment and nobody is looking for it? Many of those hunts later became articles, public projects, and queries. This book is where I bring that work together and explain what led me to each investigation. This is not a book built by following an existing framework or repeating ideas from other books. It comes from personal experience: investigations I have worked on, queries I have written, things that did not work as expected, and lessons I learned by doing the job. I do not want you to copy a query, run it, and stop there. I want you to understand why the hunt started, what evidence to look for, and how to turn the result into something useful. If this book makes you more curious about your own environment and encourages you to start looking before an alert tells you something is wrong, then it has done its job. That became CYBER HUNTER PROJECT. The idea was to create the kind of Threat Hunting reference I would like to have next to me while working: practical, easy to navigate and focused on investigations rather than hundreds of pages of theory. The book contains 32 practical Threat Hunting investigations across Email, Endpoints, Networks, Threat Intelligence, Identity, Software and Cloud Applications. The scenarios are very different. You will find hunts around Phishing, unusual email activity, suspicious process execution, DNS behaviour, network connections, authentication anomalies, software running across the environment, Threat Intelligence and activity inside Cloud Applications. But the important part for me was not simply providing a query for each case. What you will find inside When I started putting CYBER HUNTER PROJECT together, one thing was clear to me: I did not want to create a book full of theory and then add a few queries at the end. I wanted to build something practical. Something close to what we actually do when we sit in front of the telemetry and start asking questions. That is why the main part of the book is built around 32 Threat Hunting investigations across Email, Endpoints, Networks, Threat Intelligence, Identity, Software and Cloud Applications. Something else I wanted to include is what happens after we find something. Can this behaviour become a detection? Can we stop what is happening? Did it actually have an impact? Can we respond? This is where the Detection Opportunities and the HUNTER Decision Cycle come into the book. The methodology throughout the book is vendor-neutral, while the companion queries are written in KQL, simply because this is the technology I work with every day. The idea is not to copy/paste them and call it done. Take the logic, test it, change it and adapt it to your own environment. So inside the book you will find investigations, queries, diagrams, Detection Opportunities and, especially, ideas that hopefully give you another place to start your next hunt. That was the goal when I started putting all of this together. Beyond the investigations So that is what you will find inside CYBER HUNTER PROJECT: real hunting scenarios, the thinking behind them, evidence analysis and Detection Opportunities that you can adapt to your own environment. A book designed to be read, but also to stay next to your computer when you need an idea for your next hunt. 📔 CYBER HUNTER PROJECT is now available on Amazon. items.title: Hackers Hijack Coder Registry to Push Malicious Terraform Modules and Steal Cloud Credentials
items.summary: A critical security incident at Coder exposed users of its Terraform module registry to malicious packages designed to steal credentials from cloud development environments. The attack involved unauthorized changes to Coder’s Cloudflare infrastructure, allowing an unidentified threat actor to redirect some registry traffic to attacker-controlled servers. According to Coder’s security advisory, the attacker added unauthorized IP addresses to the infrastructure pool used by the Coder module registry. Those servers hosted a rogue registry containing modified Terraform artifacts with credential-stealing code. The affected service was Coder’s main registry, registry.coder.com, which is commonly used as a source of workspace templates and modules. The malicious packages were available between 07:35 UTC and 21:45 UTC on August 31, 2026. Organizations may have been exposed if they created a new Coder workspace template, updated an existing template version, ran a template dry run, or deployed a workspace. items.title: New InjectEave Attack Allows Hackers to Recover Audio Playing on Headphones from 30 Meters
items.summary: Researchers have unveiled a novel electromagnetic (EM) attack called InjectEave that lets an adversary eavesdrop on audio playing through wired and wireless headphones from as far as 30 meters away, even through walls, using nothing more than commercially available radio-frequency equipment. The technique, developed by a team from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University, was published as “Injected and Leaked: Actively Inducing Side-Channel Leakage Using Electromagnetic Injection and Hardware Nonlinearity,” accepted at USENIX Security ’26. InjectEave Attack Recovers Headphone Audio From 30 Meters Unlike traditional EM side-channel attacks , which passively sniff stray electromagnetic emissions leaking from a device, InjectEave actively injects a tuned radio-frequency carrier signal into the target device. This injected signal interacts with nonlinear hardware components inside everyday electronics, such as audio amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), power converters, and switching MOSFETs, which are ubiquitous in headphones, smart home gadgets, and landline phones. These components unintentionally “mix” the secret analog signal, like an audio waveform, with the injected carrier, effectively piggybacking the low-frequency secret onto a much higher-frequency EM wave that can travel far beyond what passive eavesdropping would allow. Injection-Induced EM Side-channel Overview The researchers describe this as an “Injection-Modulation-Emission” model, where the injected carrier couples into a device’s internal circuitry, mixes with the secret signal through hardware nonlinearity, and then re-radiates from the same wires and cables that acted as unintentional antennas in the first place. Crucially, the leaked signal’s strength scales almost linearly with both the secret signal’s amplitude and the attacker’s injection power, meaning a more powerful transmitter directly translates into a stronger, more recoverable eavesdropping signal. Conventional EM side-channel eavesdropping has always been constrained by a fundamental physics problem: secrets like human speech occupy frequencies between 20 Hz and 20 kHz, while efficient EM radiation from a device’s wiring typically requires frequencies in the megahertz-to-gigahertz range. This mismatch has historically kept passive audio eavesdropping distances limited to under 1.5 meters in prior research such as MagEar and Periscope. InjectEave sidesteps this barrier entirely by actively shaping the leakage instead of just listening for it, allowing attackers to select and tune an optimal injection frequency for each target device. Using an Ettus USRP B210 software-defined radio, log-periodic antennas, and a spectrum analyzer, the research team tested InjectEave against 11 commercial off-the-shelf devices, including wired headphones from Sony, Dell, and Apple, wireless headphones from UGreen, Philips, and HP, a Flyingvoice VoIP landline, and smart fans and lamps from Xiaomi and other brands. At a baseline distance of 50 centimeters, the attack achieved near-100% audio recognition rates across almost every audio device tested, with signal-to-noise ratios ranging from about 6 dB for Apple Earbuds to over 23 dB for the UGreen MAX2 wireless headphones. InjectEave Feasibility Testing Setup When the team swapped in an external power amplifier costing roughly $415, boosting injection power from 18 dBm to 40 dBm, the effective eavesdropping range on the UGreen MAX2 and Philips TAH2020 headphones extended to a striking 30 meters, all while remaining able to recover intelligible speech. The attack also proved resilient against physical barriers: glass and wood caused negligible signal loss of 1 to 2 dB, while even solid concrete walls only reduced signal strength by around 5.8 dB for headphones, enabling reliable through-wall eavesdropping in offices, hotels, and conference rooms. Attack Parameter Passive EM Eavesdropping (Prior Art) InjectEave Active EM Injection Methodology Listens for stray EM leakage Actively injects RF carrier to induce mixing Typical Range < 1.5 meters Up to 30 meters with external amplifier Barrier Penetration Highly degraded by walls Penetrates solid concrete with minimal loss (~5.8 dB) Required Hardware Software-defined radio (SDR) and antennas SDR, antennas, and RF power amplifier (~$415) Vulnerable Components High-frequency digital buses (HDMI, etc.) Analog amplifiers, ADCs, and power converters Target Examples PC monitors, smart speakers Headphones, landline phones, smart lamps/fans As detailed in the technical disclosure published in ArXiv , the study’s teardown analysis found that twisted-pair cabling reduced leakage by up to 20 dB compared to standard parallel wiring, offering hardware manufacturers a practical, if partial, mitigation path going forward. Perhaps most alarming, the researchers demonstrated a closed-loop “Eavesdrop-Synthesize-Inject” attack against a Flyingvoice landline phone. In this scenario, the attacker first eavesdrops on one party’s voice to build context, clones that voice using an AI voice-cloning tool called IndexTTS-2 upon detecting trigger keywords like “quote” or “confirmation,” and then injects synthesized, deepfaked audio back into the target’s headset, all in real time. Testing showed the injected fake audio was nearly indistinguishable from the original speaker’s voice, with only a 0.071 average deviation in a standard speech-intelligibility metric. To improve audio clarity from the inherently noisy, harmonic-distorted leaked signal, the team built InjectEave’s signal-enhancement module around a diffusion-based speech-denoising model trained on physics-simulated data, boosting recovered audio’s signal-to-noise ratio from 7.0 dB to 16.1 dB and its intelligibility score from 0.58 to 0.72. The attack isn’t limited to headphones. The same principle exposed power consumption patterns of smart lamps and fans, letting attackers remotely infer a household’s activity patterns, sleep schedules, and appliance usage without any network access. The researchers also found early evidence that microphone inputs are vulnerable, though currently limited to roughly 30 centimeters due to microphones’ much weaker signal levels. Existing defenses like cryptographic masking and EM shielding largely fail here, since InjectEave targets continuous analog signals rather than digital logic, and a determined attacker can simply crank up injection power to overcome standard shielding. The researchers stress that comprehensive, security-aware hardware-software co-design will be needed to close this newly exposed analog attack surface across headphones, IoT devices, and beyond. items.title: Cloud Native Computing Foundation Announces Karmada Graduation
items.summary: Multi-cluster, multi-cloud Kubernetes orchestration project reaches production maturity as global enterprises scale AI training and inference across hybrid infrastructure Key Highlights Karmada has graduated from the CNCF, recognizing the project’s maturity as an open source engine for orchestrating applications across multiple Kubernetes clusters, clouds, and regions without modifying the applications themselves. Karmada v1.19 release advances multi-component scheduling for distributed AI training jobs. Global enterprises and leading cloud, telecom, and AI platforms, including Bloomberg, Wellhub, Alibaba Cloud, Huawei, and Trip.com , rely on Karmada for hybrid cloud capacity, multi-region resilience, and multi-cluster  AI infrastructure. SHANGHAI, China – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 – September 8, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announces the graduation of Karmada, an open source project that lets organizations run applications across multiple Kubernetes clusters, clouds, and regions without changing the applications themselves. This milestone comes as Karmada advances multi-cluster AI infrastructure through its v1.19 release , which advances multi-component scheduling for distributed AI training jobs and promotes priority-based scheduling to Beta, enabled by default, to ensure critical workloads are scheduled first. The project’s production footprint now powers mission-critical infrastructure for a diverse global adopter base, ranging from global enterprises like Bloomberg and Wellhub to major cloud, telecom, and AI platforms across Asia. “As organizations scale Kubernetes across clusters and GPU constrained AI environments, having a production ready way to coordinate that fleet becomes critical to operational success,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “Reaching CNCF graduation demonstrates that Karmada has achieved the technical maturity, governance, and security work required for the enterprise; we look forward to seeing the project continue to grow within the ecosystem.” Short for Kubernetes Armada, Karmada extends the standard Kubernetes API with centralized placement, propagation, failover, and multi-cluster autoscaling. Karmada’s CNCF history dates back to its first commit in November 2020. The project then officially joined in September 2021 as a Sandbox project before advancing to Incubating status in December 2023. Since joining CNCF, Karmada has grown to more than 1,214 contributors across 292 contributing organizations and more than 5,600 GitHub stars. Its production adopter base includes a significant portion of Chinese cloud, internet, telecom, AI, travel, logistics, device, and enterprise organizations, including Alibaba Cloud, Bilibili, Huawei, iFLYTEK, JDCloud, Kuaishou, RedNote, SenseTime, Trip.com, Vivo, WPS, and ZTO, alongside global adopters like Bloomberg and Wellhub. These companies use Karmada to support hybrid cloud capacity, multi-region resilience, intelligent traffic distribution, AI training, GPU/CPU scheduling, multi-cluster application delivery, and fleet-wide service-configuration distribution. Karmada also integrates directly with existing CNCF observability and deployment projects: it exports Prometheus metrics across its control-plane components, packages an etcd instance for control-plane state, and ships Helm charts for installation. “I am proud that Karmada has grown into critical infrastructure that large enterprises count on — powering everything from microservices to big data and AI,” said Hongcai Ren, Karmada maintainer. “None of this would have happened without the open, neutral platform CNCF built, where adopters and developers explore this space side by side. Graduation is a new starting point: we look forward to partnering with more adopters, learning from richer real-world scenarios, and working with the broader ecosystem to tackle the challenges of AI and agent infrastructure together.” Karmada’s broader 2026 roadmap builds on that foundation, moving multi-cluster Kubernetes from basic workload propagation toward a more resource-aware control plane. It also includes priority-based preemption, multi-cluster queuing for AI training and batch jobs, and multi-cluster support for Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) across GPUs and other accelerators. To reach graduation status, Karmada completed a third-party security audit, established a formal steering committee to ensure transparent governance, and adopted the CNCF Code of Conduct . The project also maintains a Core Infrastructure Initiative (CII) Best Practices Badge, demonstrating a commitment to secure software development. The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) provides technical leadership to the cloud native community, defining its vision and stewarding projects through maturity levels up to graduation. The announcement was made during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 , where these three Foundations convened together in China for the first time on a single stage, underscoring the growing need for multi-cluster orchestration that spans private data centers, public clouds, and specialized AI hardware. Supporting Quotes “As organizations scale beyond a single Kubernetes cluster, they need consistent management without added complexity. Karmada solves this by extending familiar Kubernetes APIs to work across clusters and clouds. With maintainers across six organizations and adopters running it at significant scale, we congratulate Karmada on its successful graduation as a CNCF project,” – Chad Beaudin, TOC Sponsor. “Karmada has become foundational to how Bloomberg operates resilient cloud native infrastructure. By automating disaster recovery, improving resource utilization, and simplifying the management of individual Kubernetes clusters, it has enabled our platform engineering teams to operate more efficiently, while also giving internal application teams a simpler, more consistent experience deploying jobs. As close collaborators with the Karmada community over the past few years, we have seen this open source project continue to evolve, and its graduation reflects its growing importance to enterprise organizations that are managing complex Kubernetes environments.” – Michas Szacillo, Engineering Team Lead of Bloomberg’s Streaming Platform and Karmada maintainer “At Trip.com , Karmada has become a critical part of our multi-cluster infrastructure and has delivered significant value in production. Without changing existing Kubernetes resource definitions, it has enabled us to operate multiple clusters as a unified resource pool, support cross-cluster elasticity and failover, bring new clusters into production more efficiently, and perform large-scale workload migration with minimal disruption to applications. This has greatly reduced the complexity of operating infrastructure at scale. As computing increasingly spans regions, clouds, and heterogeneous resources, we believe Karmada will become an essential foundation for reliable and scalable cloud-native and AI infrastructure.” – Honghui Yue, Senior Development Expert, Trip.com “Karmada powers multi-cluster orchestration in DaoCloud’s enterprise platform, helping customers implement multi-cloud strategies through a consistent, Kubernetes-native experience across clusters and environments. Compatibility with Kubernetes APIs and existing toolchains makes it practical for production, while our community participation turns customer feedback into upstream improvements. We are extending this foundation to our AI Token Factory architecture as multi-cluster inference across data centers becomes increasingly important. Graduation gives us greater confidence in Karmada as a long-term foundation, and we look forward to contributing more capabilities for production AI inference,” – Kay Yan, Chief Architect, DaoCloud . For more information about Karmada, visit https://karmada.io/ . About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private, and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io . ### Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io

items.title: China Merchants Bank Wins CNCF End User Case Study Contest for Unifying AI Training and Inference on Kubernetes
items.summary: New cloud native platform lifted average accelerator compute utilization from 35% to more than 60% and cut inference cost per 1 million tokens by more than 60% Key Highlights China Merchants Bank, one of China’s leading commercial banks, won the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026. The award recognizes the bank’s unified Kubernetes control plane built with Kueue, KEDA, Prometheus, HAMi, and Fluid that lets AI training, fine-tuning, and online inference share nearly 10,000 heterogeneous accelerator cards. Bringing 99% of its accelerator compute resources under this framework lifted average utilization from 35% to more than 60% and cut the cost of processing 1 million tokens (input and output combined) by more than 60%. The bank’s in-house Twinkle training framework lets five LoRA tenants share one base model instance by default, cutting accelerator resource usage for that setup by 80% while increasing training density by fivefold. SHANGHAI, China – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 – September 8, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation ® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced China Merchants Bank, one of China’s leading commercial banks, as the winner of the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 . “As AI workloads continue to expand to critical infrastructure sectors such as financial, the core technology supporting it has to work harder without multiplying cost,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “China Merchants Bank’s approach to unifying AI training and inference is a clear example of how composable, vendor neutral infrastructure powered by CNCF projects delivers measurable efficiency at scale.” China Merchants Bank’s AI infrastructure team built a unified control plane by combining Kubernetes with Kueue , KEDA , Prometheus , HAMi , and Fluid , letting model training, fine-tuning, and online inference share nearly 10,000 heterogeneous accelerator cards. Through close collaboration with its data center and other teams, the bank brought 99% of its accelerator compute resources under this unified framework — lifting average utilization across those nearly 10,000 cards from 35% to more than 60%, while cutting the cost of processing 1 million tokens (input and output combined) by more than 60% under comparable model and service conditions. “At China Merchants Bank, we unlock the potential of hardware through software innovation,” said  PeiXiang Tan, AI Infrastructure Architect, China Merchants Bank. “Built on a unified cloud-native foundation, our platform brings together heterogeneous compute pooling, training job scheduling, elastic inference scaling, accelerated access to data and models, and end-to-end observability. This allows training and inference to follow workload-specific paths while working in close coordination—helping every unit of compute deliver greater value over time. ” With AI adoption expanding across more financial use cases, China Merchants Bank found that training, inference, and multi-tenant fine-tuning place significantly different demands on the same hardware. Distributed training requires stable, predictable capacity that can sit idle while waiting for remaining workers or accelerator cards to become available, while online inference needs to scale quickly with unpredictable traffic. To address these competing demands, the bank built a composable architecture that shares infrastructure while decoupling runtimes: Kueue manages training admission, queues, and quotas so jobs don’t reserve capacity before they can use it; KEDA and Prometheus scale online inference from live demand signals; HAMi allocates shared accelerator capacity in fine-grained units across both paths; and Fluid accelerates access to datasets, model weights, and checkpoints so accelerators spend less time waiting on data. China Merchants Bank’s in-house Twinkle training framework adds another layer of efficiency for multi-tenant fine-tuning, letting five LoRA tenants share one base-model instance by default. Reducing base-model replicas from five to one cuts accelerator resource usage for this setup by 80% while increasing training density fivefold. China Merchants Bank has published previous CNCF case studies on its AI infrastructure work, including one detailing a Kubernetes and HAMi-based scheduling platform that achieved 100% hardware pool utilization through topology-aware scheduling and a 30% reduction in cross-machine scheduling for distributed training workloads. China Merchants Bank plans to continue building on these advances, focusing on four key areas: adjusting multi-tenant training concurrency dynamically, combining utilization, queue state, and latency signals into unit-cost-based capacity management, extending KEDA toward serverless inference that can scale to zero between demand spikes, and broadening HAMi-based support for heterogeneous accelerators while adding more training and inference backends. China Merchants Bank’s achievement was announced on stage during a keynote at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China. SHANGHAI – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China —Sept. 8, 2026 — The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today released new findings from its latest State of Cloud Native Development in China report, in collaboration with SlashData . The research dives into China’s growing cloud native ecosystem and examines how cloud native infrastructure is supporting AI teams as they move from experimentation and training toward production inference. “AI is moving quickly but cloud native is defining the open source infrastructure that will support it in production at scale,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “China has a strong open source developer community that can play an important role in that work. As inference scales, many of the challenges look familiar to cloud native — scheduling, isolation, networking, observability and operating distributed systems reliably. Bridging these communities together is how we build an open AI infrastructure stack that developers can contribute to, build on and run anywhere.” Cloud native provides a path from AI experimentation to production The report estimates that China is home to approximately 1.75 million cloud native developers as of Q1 2026, with adoption especially resonating with the country’s next generation of developers. Professional IIoT developers in China are more likely to be cloud native (48%) than the global average (42%), signifying technical demand for complex deployments. Approximately 400,000 AI developers in China are cloud native, underscoring the intersection between the country’s cloud native and AI developer ecosystems. The global cloud native developer community has reached 19.9 million developers and continues to grow. Nearly half (48%) of Chinese backend developers are now classified as cloud native, up from 30% two years ago. Compared to the global rate of 52%, China has rapidly reached the global baseline. Both China and the global tech community are taking notice of cloud native’s role in AI. The report examines how AI developers adopt infrastructure technologies as their workloads mature. Developers follow a distinct cloud native path: Data pipeline operations: Kubernetes and microservices provide the foundational infrastructure layer, followed by event-driven architecture, streaming services and observability tools to support sophisticated data pipelines. Training and experimentation: Feature flagging, RPC and immutable infrastructure support model version routing, distributed training and reproducible environments. Production serving: Service meshes, chaos engineering and multicluster management support traffic splitting, resilience testing and distributed inference at scale. As AI systems move toward production, specific cloud native practices will continue to support different requirements. China’s new generation of developers embrace cloud native Similar to recent CNCF and SlashData findings from India , adoption in China is particularly strong among younger developers with more than half of Chinese backend developers under age 45 classified as cloud native. Among backend developers under 25, that figure reaches 58%, suggesting cloud native is embedded in how the next generation builds backend services. “China’s developer ecosystem offers an important view into how cloud native adoption is evolving alongside AI and industrial development,” said Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData. “The strong adoption among younger backend developers points to cloud native becoming an increasingly established part of modern software development, while our global AI findings show how these infrastructure practices evolve as teams progress toward increasingly sophisticated production AI systems.” Infrastructure becomes more crucial as AI matures Platform engineering is changing how developers interact with underlying cloud native infrastructure. 88% of backend developers now work with some form of infrastructure standardization, up from 80% six months ago. As platforms abstract technologies such as Kubernetes and containers, the underlying infrastructure can become less visible to developers even as it becomes more critical to production workloads. At the most advanced levels of cloud native maturity, these practices converge. The report found the strongest technology association in the dataset between immutable infrastructure and chaos engineering, with a lift of 2.22. This means the two are adopted together at more than twice the rate. This “elite cluster” also includes multicluster management and service meshes, which shows how developers who operate complex systems adopt multiple advanced infrastructure practices. For AI teams, the maturity path looks different. Immutable infrastructure emerges early on to support consistent deployments, while more advanced production environments bring together chaos engineering, service meshes, and multicluster management to support areas like resiliency and distributed inference. As AI becomes deeply embedded in production systems, the data reinforces the growing role of cloud native technologies as the infrastructure base for the AI-native era. This “elite cluster” also includes multicluster management and service meshes, which shows how developers who operate complex systems adopt multiple advanced infrastructure practices.

For AI teams, the maturity path looks different. Immutable infrastructure emerges early on to support consistent deployments, while more advanced production environments bring together chaos engineering, service meshes, and multicluster management to support areas like resiliency and distributed inference. As AI becomes deeply embedded in production systems, the data reinforces the growing role of cloud native technologies as the infrastructure base for the AI-native era.
